title: Human gates
point: Place human approval by cost of error and reversibility, so people review the few actions that matter instead of rubber-stamping everything.
definition: A human gate is a control point where a person checks an agent action. Gates differ in timing: approve before the action, review a sample after it, or forbid the action for agents entirely.

objective.text: Sort agent actions into automatic, review-after, approve-before and never, justify each by reversibility, external effect and value, and estimate the reviewer load the placement creates.

misconceptions.claim: Requiring approval for every action is the safest design.
misconceptions.correction: Reviewers facing hundreds of low-risk approvals start clicking yes without reading. Approval fatigue turns every gate into a rubber stamp, including the gates that matter.

misconceptions.claim: A human gate stops prompt injection on its own.
misconceptions.correction: It helps only if the reviewer sees the real effect, such as recipient, amount and content. A vague summary written by the same model can hide the attack.

l1: Auto: reversible, low-value, internal actions run without a person, and every action is logged. Reading a public catalogue or labelling a ticket fits here.
Review-after: cheap actions that can be undone run immediately, and a person reviews a sample later. A $15 refund within policy is a typical case.
Approve-before: irreversible, external or high-value actions wait for a person. Never: actions no agent may take, such as changing payout bank details because an email asked.
l2: Score each action with three questions. Can it be undone? Does its effect leave the organisation? What does one wrong action cost?
Deleting an account cannot be undone, so it waits for approval. Rescheduling a delivery is reversible and cheap, so it runs and is sampled.
Show the reviewer the exact effect: recipient, amount, data fields and the evidence the agent used. Approve the action itself, not the agent's description of it.
l3: Budget reviewer time. If 2 per cent of 5,000 daily actions need approval at one minute each, that is 100 minutes of review a day.
Track approval rate and time to decide. Near 100 per cent approval with decisions under three seconds suggests rubber-stamping, so move low-risk actions down a tier.
Every gate needs a timeout rule. Decide what happens when nobody approves in time; usually the action is cancelled and the requester is told.
